Supervised learning means learning from examples where the answer is already known:
casts where the water mass was identified, hauls where the catch was recorded, images
where a specialist labelled the species. The model learns the relationship between the
inputs and the answer, then applies it to cases where the answer is unknown. This is
the family of methods most marine work needs.

The kind of answer comes first, because it decides which models fit and how their
errors are scored. [Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) split
the task into regression, for a quantity, and classification, for a category. Few
marine outcomes fit either box neatly:

| Outcome | What needs care |
| --- | --- |
| Catch weight | Skewed: a few very large catches |
| Count of animals | Whole numbers, never negative, with a spread that grows with the average |
| Count with many zeros | A zero can mean the species is absent, or present and missed |
| Percentage cover | Cannot go below 0 or above 100 |
| Present or absent | One of the two is usually much rarer |
| Habitat class | Often ordered (poor, fair, good), and the order carries information |

Turning a quantity into a category, such as a count into present or absent, makes it
simpler but throws information away;
[Logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd#a-probability-stays-between-0-and-1)
shows what goes.

The section then introduces one method per page, each on the same simulated survey, so
each new method can be compared with the ones before it:

- linear and polynomial regression for a quantity, a straight line and then a curve,
  the yardstick for everything after;
- Poisson and negative binomial regression for a count, which never predict fewer than
  zero animals;
- logistic regression for a yes-or-no outcome, such as present or absent;
- k-nearest neighbours, which predicts from the most similar stations and assumes no
  shape;
- decision trees, which predict by asking yes-or-no questions about the inputs;
- random forests and boosting, which combine many trees into one prediction.

It ends on choosing between them. The aim, the kind of outcome, the range the model
must predict over, the amount of data and the people who must accept the result all
narrow the choice before any model is fitted. Comparing the section's models on the
same new sites then shows why one test split cannot settle a close contest, which
[Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) takes up.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [Build a model](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/models/), tidymodels. One model specification, several engines.
- [Search parsnip models](https://www.tidymodels.org/find/parsnip/), tidymodels. Which methods have a `parsnip` interface and what each engine needs.
- [Supervised learning](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/supervised_learning.html), scikit-learn user guide. The whole menu, with [linear models](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html) and [ensembles](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html) as the two that matter here.
